# Save and combine your plots

**The question:** how do I get a figure *out* of R — at paper quality — and put several
plots together into one multi-panel figure?

The trick runs through the whole workshop: **assign every plot to an object** (`p <- ggplot(...)`).
Once a plot is an object you can save it, reuse it, and combine it.

## Setup {-}

```{r setup08, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)   # here() builds paths from the project root, so they work wherever you run this
library(patchwork)
meta <- read_tsv(here("project/data", "metadata.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
de   <- read_tsv(here("project/data", "DE_biofilm_vs_planktonic_24h.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# Two plots, each saved to an OBJECT so we can save and combine them.
samples_plot <- ggplot(meta, aes(x = lifestyle, fill = timepoint)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Samples", x = NULL, y = "n")

de_plot <- de %>%
  mutate(padj = ifelse(padj == 0, min(padj[padj > 0], na.rm = TRUE), padj),
         status = case_when(padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange >  1 ~ "Up",
                            padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange < -1 ~ "Down",
                            TRUE                              ~ "ns"))
volcano <- ggplot(de_plot, aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj), colour = status)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Biofilm vs planktonic")
```

## Save a plot at paper resolution

`ggsave()` writes the last plot — or any plot object — to a file. The **file extension
picks the format**, and you set the **size** and, for raster formats, the **resolution**.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Raster (PNG) — needs a resolution. 300 dpi is the usual minimum for print.
ggsave("volcano.png", plot = volcano, width = 8.9, height = 8, units = "cm", dpi = 300)

# Vector (PDF or SVG) — infinitely sharp, and editable in Illustrator / Inkscape.
ggsave("volcano.pdf", plot = volcano, width = 8.9, height = 8, units = "cm")
```

<div class="note">
  <strong>📘 Note — journal sizes:</strong> many journals want figures sized to the column.
  Nature, for example: <strong>8.9 cm</strong> single column, <strong>18.3 cm</strong>
  double column. Set <code>width</code> to those and the text won't shrink when the figure
  is placed.
</div>

<div class="important">
  <strong>⭐ Important:</strong> for a figure you'll tweak later (in Illustrator/Inkscape)
  or submit to a journal, export **vector** (<code>.pdf</code> or <code>.svg</code>) — it
  stays sharp at any size. Use <strong>PNG at 300 dpi</strong> only when you need an image
  (slides, web).
</div>

## Combine plots with patchwork

The `patchwork` package lets you add plots together like a formula:

```{r}
samples_plot + volcano          # side by side
```

```{r}
samples_plot / volcano          # stacked (one on top of the other)
```

Add panel labels (A, B, …) with `plot_annotation`:

```{r}
(samples_plot | volcano) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

<div class="tip">
  <strong>💡 Tip:</strong> if two panels share a legend, collapse it to one with
  <code>plot_layout(guides = "collect")</code>.
</div>

A combined figure is itself a plot object, so you save it the same way:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
figure <- (samples_plot | volcano) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
ggsave("figure_1.pdf", plot = figure, width = 18.3, height = 8, units = "cm")
```

<div class="remember">
  <strong>📌 Principle:</strong> assign plots to objects → then you can <em>save</em> them
  (<code>ggsave</code>, vector for print) and <em>combine</em> them (<code>patchwork</code>)
  into publication-ready, multi-panel figures.
</div>

### 👉 Your turn {-}

Stack `volcano` on top of `samples_plot`, label the panels A and B, and save the result
as a **PDF at double-column width** (18.3 cm).

<details>
<summary>Solution</summary>
```{r, eval=FALSE}
fig <- (volcano / samples_plot) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
ggsave("my_figure.pdf", plot = fig, width = 18.3, height = 16, units = "cm")
```
</details>

> 🤖 **Ask your AI:** *"With patchwork, how do I make the left panel twice as wide as the
> right one?"*
